body.text: There is a young woman who writes beautifully. Her words touch the heart and resonate in the mind. She has lived all her life in Colaba, Mumbai. Her first name is Sana. My youngest daughter is also named Sana. It is a Semitic word found in all the three great religions of Palestine: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. It derives from the Hebrew word “Hosanna”, which means “praise”: praise to the Creator for the miracle and mystery of birth and life and all that we call Nature. As a given name it is much in contemporary use in the Muslim world. But to find it coupled with a Hindu surname is rare—Krishna in this girl’s case and Aiyar in my daughter’s case.

My daughter is called Sana because she was born in Karachi during my posting there as a diplomat. Her two older sisters had a senior with this name in school whom they greatly admired. That is how our Sana became Sana. In Sana Krishna’s case, neither of her parents is Muslim and she was born in Mumbai. It was her Zoroastrian mother who gave Sana Krishna her first name, adding a fourth religion to those who celebrate hamd-us-sana, “The Glory of God”. She took her surname from her Hindu father.

But it is not her parents of whom she writes, but of her beloved “Dada”, her paternal grandfather who used to ready her for school, then wait in the melting heat for her to emerge from class and carry her back home on his shoulders, regaling her with stories from his lost youth—lost because he was raised in that part of Punjab, in and around Lahore, which became Pakistan. And as a young adult, he had to leave everything behind, including his friends and memories, to save his life.
This rang a bell in my head as I too was born in Lahore, where my Tamil father had lived for 20 years but was forced to reluctantly uproot his life when the country was vivisected.

Sana writes: “I did not think of Dada as a refugee. He was simply my grandfather. His Lahore was simply a place where he had once lived. Partition belonged to history books, black-and-white photographs and stories from another era. Only much later did I begin to understand that the gentleness I associated with him was inseparable from the generation he belonged to.”

Dada had bought a chair for the chowkidar to sit on during the long hours he daily guarded the gates. It is that characteristic of gentleness that she invokes of an era which the rest of us associate with the horrific violence that rent asunder people and their forefathers who had known each other intimately and remembered with great fondness their lives together.

She invokes also their resilience as they rebuilt their lives in lands they had known nothing about: “Who opened the first shop? Who found the first job? Who created recipes from memory?” And poignantly concludes the passage: “Distance has a peculiar way of making inherited histories visible.” I think we have discovered Gen Z’s Arundhati Roy.

She goes on: “Our food is mirrored flavours. Our music is mirrored longings. Our memories are often mirrored landscapes.” Sana regrets our having to interpret “every relationship through a national border” and speculates that “perhaps our responsibility is to stop treating the recognition of shared humanity as a betrayal”.
What she wants her generation to “keep discovering” is “that the stranger on the other side of the border speaks in a voice that sounds unexpectedly like home”.
Jigar Moradabadi had anticipated her:
“Unka jo kaam hai, woh
Ahl-e-siyasat jaane/
Mera paigham mohabbat hai,
Jahan tak pahunche.”
(“Let the politicians, whose job it is,
Get on with it/
My message is Love,
As far as it might spread”)

A senior statesman, much involved with foreign affairs, has refuted the relevance of these sentimentalities. After lauding Sana Krishna for her beautiful writing and feelings, he deplores her “disingenuous” question: “Who exactly are we protecting ourselves from?” and answers: “From the malign men in uniform in Rawalpindi GHQ.” Really?

As it is unlikely that Sana will be able to give an answer from a history she has not lived, I give myself the liberty, as a doddering 85-year-old croc who has spent 50 years immersed in our relationship with Pakistan, to try to give a clarification.

Radcliffe divided the land. He did not divide the waters. That was left to the politicians of the day. For a decade or more, they could not agree. They knew how to squabble, not how to resolve. Then came a military dictator, Field Marshal Ayub Khan. He bluntly told our High Commissioner, Rajeshwar Dayal, that as he had the politicians “by their balls” he would reach a mutually acceptable agreement on the division of the Indus waters.

Under the aegis of this man in uniform, India and Pakistan reached a treaty that both countries accepted and observed notwithstanding all the wars that followed over the next seven decades. The treaty has now been stranded in “abeyance”, not because of any men in uniform in Rawalpindi but because of a man in kurta-pyjama-jacket who lives in New Delhi.

We then had to deal with a highly popular and democratically elected civilian leader of Pakistan, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto. He first provoked a “thousand-year war” on “Hindu” India and then betrayed India over the Simla Agreement. Malign men in civvies are also to be found outside Rawalpindi GHQ. This malignant civilian was thankfully overthrown in 1977 by a military man, Zia-ul-Haq, remembered by almost all Pakistanis and many Indians as perhaps the most malignant of the men in uniform.
Most fruitful years

Yet, it was he who jointly inaugurated, with Prime Minister Morarji Desai, what were perhaps the most fruitful years in India-Pakistan relations. It was a time when everything that Sana Krishna desires actually happened. And it happened under my own eyes. I issued over 3 lakh visas and not one was misused. In return, I was greeted with cries in our visa waiting hall of “Hindustan ke Consul-General zindabad, zindabad! Yahan koi rishwat nahin/koi pabandi nahin”. As the Beatles sang, “All you need is love, love is all you need”.

Military dictatorship is terrible for Pakistanis. Yet, it is only such military dictators who have the clout to settle with India. But we persist in the absurd demand that India will choose who it wishes to represent Pakistan. We deal with all kinds of vicious characters around the world. We even embrace the Taliban in Afghanistan.

And, therefore, we blot out of our own and public memory the constructive moments in our relations with GHQ, Rawalpindi. Of these, perhaps the most important was the near conclusion of the “four-point” agreement on Kashmir when Gen. Pervez Musharraf held the reins of power. It was the outcome of Atal Bihari Vajpayee, followed by Dr Manmohan Singh, consciously deciding that we had to deal with whoever the Pakistani system puts in office. Diplomacy has to grapple with reality, not fantasy. We cannot choose our counterpart.

Remember how it was under the previous Pakistani army chief, Gen. Qamar Javed Bajwa (2016-22), regarded by Pakistani public opinion as among the most nefarious of their military chiefs. On his watch, the same Narendra Modi government, which ostentatiously refuses to talk to Pakistan, concluded with the men in uniform the Kartarpur opening to our Sikh brethren and the agreement to strictly observe the ceasefire line in Kashmir. Did Bajwa leave his malignancy behind in Rawalpindi GHQ?

The truth of the matter is that it is the blameless people of India and Pakistan who are kept from reconciling with each other by the “Ahl-e-siyasat”. What Sana Krishna seeks is that ordinary folk who wish to reconcile with each other as fellow human beings be permitted to get on with their goodwill blitz, even as governments get on with their job of targeting each other as monsters.

Mani Shankar Aiyar served 26 years in the Indian Foreign Service, is a four-time MP with over two decades in Parliament, and was a Cabinet Minister from 2004 to 2009. He has published nine books, the latest, A Maverick in Politics, the second part of his memoir.
